definition: Able to work well in practice, or able to live and grow.
example: After months of testing, the engineers finally had a viable design for a cheaper battery.
nuance: Feasible means something can be done; viable means it can actually succeed or survive once it is done.
prompt: A student council is deciding how to raise money for a new school garden.
options: Selling seedlings at the spring fair was the most viable plan the council found.
The plan was viable because it would cost far more than the council could ever hope to raise.
The posters were so viable that everyone in the hallway noticed them.
The treasurer felt viable after a long nap before the meeting.
reasons: A cheap fundraiser that can realistically bring in money is a plan that can succeed.
A plan nobody can afford is bound to fail, so this reverses the meaning.
This confuses the word with visible; being easy to see says nothing about working.
The word judges whether a plan or living thing can last, not a person's mood or energy.

practice.prompt: A gardener checks whether seeds from an old packet will still sprout.
options: The seeds were viable, so none of them sprouted no matter how much water they got.
The gardener picked the most viable seeds because their bright colors stood out on the table.
Her excuse for forgetting to water the pots was viable enough that her neighbor believed it.
Only a few seeds from the dusty packet were still viable, so just three sprouts appeared.
reasons: Seeds that never sprout cannot grow, so this flips the meaning.
Standing out to the eye is about visibility, not about the ability to grow.
This confuses the word with plausible; a believable excuse is not one that works or grows.
Seeds that can still germinate are alive and able to grow, which fits the sense.
